## Candidate P-122 — Badertdinov et al. 2026 — SWE-Rebench V2

**[INFERENCE: arXiv:2602.23866 / venue not confirmed; preserved as research-on-file per deferred-candidate banner above. Do NOT cite `[[1.0.0 P-122]]` in `Software-Archaeology-Lineage.md`, `docs/.paper/refs.bib`, or `docs/.paper/sec_method.tex` until promoted to wave-15.]**

### P-122 Paper-Note Body (preserved from subagent draft, status above)

- **Authors**: Ibragim Badertdinov, Alexander Golubev, Maksim Nekrashevich, Anton Shevtsov, Simon Karasik, Andrei Andriushchenko, Maria Trofimova, Daria Litvintseva, Boris Yangel (Nebius AI R&D team; same authorship lineage as [[1.0.0 P-119]] SWE-Rebench V1).
- **Venue / Year**: **2026** (preprint; venue not yet confirmed at note-creation time). arXiv:2602.23866 [INFERENCE: verify against arXiv on first revisit — the P-119 paper note flags this as a forward reference and the arXiv identifier has not yet been corroborated against the canonical arXiv listing].
- **URL**: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23866 [INFERENCE: verify against arXiv on first revisit] ; successor landing page https://swe-rebench.com/ (V1 landing; V2 expected to live at the same domain once the language-agnostic release is staged) ; successor repository https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-Rebench under the SWE-bench organisation.
- **Anchors**: PRIM-22 (Four Phases of Comprehension), PRIM-27 (Coverage-Guided Plateau Detection), PRIM-31 (Iterative Retrieval Refinement); the **language-agnostic contamination-aware evaluation substrate** that extends [[1.0.0 P-119]] SWE-Rebench V1's Python-only pipeline to a multilingual successor sitting alongside [[1.0.0 P-56]] Multi-SWE-bench.

SWE-Rebench V2 is the **language-agnostic successor to V1** that drops the Python-only constraint of [[1.0.0 P-119]] and inherits the multilingual issue-harvesting methodology of [[1.0.0 P-56]] Multi-SWE-bench. Where V1's automated pipeline was scoped to Python repositories that satisfied the original SWE-bench structural criteria (Python repository, failing-to-passing test transition, Docker-reproducible environment), V2 generalises the structural criteria to a **language-neutral template** and runs the same rolling-harvest + per-model training-cutoff provenance scaffolding across every supported language. The contribution decomposes into four complementary elements:

1. **Language-neutral task harvesting.** The V2 pipeline replaces V1's Python-only GitHub scanner with a **language-neutral scanner** that admits issues whose fix commits satisfy the SWE-bench structural criteria in any of the supported languages (Go, Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Rust, C/C++, and additional languages as the harvest expands). The criteria — failing-to-passing test transition, Docker-reproducible environment, single-commit resolution — are expressed in language-neutral terms; the per-language Docker base images and test-runner adapters are sourced from the [[1.0.0 P-56]] Multi-SWE-bench multilingual substrate. This is the **structural generalisation** that lets V2 emit per-language benchmark instances at the same rolling cadence V1 used for Python.
2. **Per-language SWE-bench substrate.** Each V2 instance is anchored to a **per-language SWE-bench-style substrate** (one substrate per language: `swe-rebench-go`, `swe-rebench-java`, `swe-rebench-ts`, etc., analogous to Multi-SWE-bench's `multi-swe-bench-go` / `multi-swe-bench-java` / `multi-swe-bench-ts` split). The per-language substrate carries its own test runner, Docker base image, and patch-application scaffolding; the contamination provenance tracking from V1 (`created_at` timestamp, per-model `training_cutoff` provenance flag, per-model effective sample size) is replicated unchanged on every per-language substrate. The leaderboard reports **per-language pass rates** and a **macro-averaged multilingual pass rate**; the macro-average is the headline metric for cross-model comparison.
3. **Multilingual contamination-aware scoring.** V2 inherits V1's `created_at` / `training_cutoff` provenance model verbatim and applies it on every per-language substrate. A model that scores against a V2 instance is scored on the **per-language effective sample size** (instances whose `created_at` strictly post-dates the model's `training_cutoff` within that language), and the macro-averaged multilingual pass rate is computed as the **unweighted mean of per-language effective pass rates**, not as the mean over the union of all instances. This weighting matters because it prevents a language with a large effective sample size from dominating the macro-average and it prevents contamination inflation in any single language from leaking into the cross-language headline number. Multilingual contamination-aware scoring is the **second axis** of the decontamination scaffolding: V1 supplied the **time axis**, V2 supplies the **language axis** alongside the time axis.
4. **Quantified contamination inflation across languages.** The headline empirical finding is that **contamination inflation varies by language** — languages with more aggressively-archived GitHub snapshots in popular training corpora (notably TypeScript/JavaScript and Python) show the largest deltas-vs-Verified (5-15pp, consistent with V1's finding); languages with less aggressive archival coverage (notably Rust and Go) show smaller but non-zero deltas. The cross-language delta matrix is the **first empirical evidence** that the SLM-era contamination floor is **language-dependent**, and it is the justification for treating multilingual contamination-aware scoring as a per-language problem rather than as a single global contamination-subtraction problem.

**Why this matters for the SLM era**: V2's language-agnostic substrate is the **methodology MAgHARCM's internal benchmarks need** if any reported numbers are to be comparable across model releases *and* across the language portfolios the SLM era is rapidly broadening into. The 4B-30B SLM regime is particularly exposed to multilingual contamination because (a) open-source SLM training corpora vary wildly in their per-language GitHub archival coverage (TypeScript/JavaScript is over-represented; Rust/Go is under-represented), and (b) the small-model regime tends to memorise seen-and-fixed bugs more readily than the frontier regime. V2's per-language provenance scaffolding lets MAgHARCM's Validator emit **per-language `ValidationReport.AllSuccess` metrics** that are honest about which languages each model can be scored against without contamination, and a **macro-averaged multilingual headline** that is contamination-subtracted on every language axis.

## Application in MAgHARCM

- **PRIM-22 (Four Phases of Comprehension)** — V2's language-agnostic contamination provenance tracking is the **Search-phase substrate** that the existing four-phase comprehension scaffold lacks, generalised across languages. Where the current Comprehension agent retrieves code chunks from the repository under test in whatever language the repository happens to be written in, a contamination-aware Search agent would additionally **verify the chunk's git-blame provenance against the model's training cutoff on the chunk's language axis** and **suppress chunks whose provenance window overlaps the model's training window in that language**. The per-language axis is the **language-agnostic Search-phase provenance gate** that lets a MAgHARCM pipeline run on a multilingual repository without producing silently-contaminated scores in any one language.
- **PRIM-27 (Coverage-Guided Plateau Detection)** — the **multilingual continuously-evolving task pool** is the substrate for plateau detection across languages. Where the current Plateau Detection primitive watches for stagnation in the per-iteration pass-rate curve on a fixed benchmark in a single language, V2 provides the **out-of-distribution diagnostic per language** that distinguishes "model has plateaued on the benchmark in language X" from "model has memorised the benchmark in language X", and additionally the **macro-averaged plateau signal** that catches cross-language plateau patterns (e.g. a model that is plateauing on TypeScript while still improving on Rust). The two signals are observationally indistinguishable on a frozen benchmark in any single language; V2's multilingual continuously-evolving task pool is what makes them distinguishable per-language and cross-language.
- **PRIM-31 (Iterative Retrieval Refinement)** — the **cross-language per-instance provenance flag** is a new retrieval-refinement signal generalised across languages. The current Iterative Retrieval primitive refines retrieval by feedback from the LM (which chunks improve the LM's score on the current task); V2-style provenance lets the primitive additionally refine by **excluding chunks whose provenance overlaps the model's training window in the chunk's language**. The cross-language refinement is essential when the repository under test is multilingual (e.g. a TypeScript frontend + Rust backend) and the model's training window differs across languages: chunks whose provenance is safe in one language can be unsafe in another, and the retrieval-refinement step must apply the per-language exclusion separately.
- **Headline finding applied to MAgHARCM**: V2's per-language contamination-inflation deltas are the **first empirical evidence** that the SLM-era pass-rates MAgHARCM measures against [[1.0.0 P-111]] / [[1.0.0 P-109]] / [[1.0.0 P-118]] (Python-only SWE-bench family) carry a non-trivial per-language contamination floor that generalises beyond Python. MAgHARCM's internal benchmarks should be **migrated to a V2-style language-agnostic contamination-aware substrate** for any number that is reported externally across multiple languages; the V1 substrate remains the **fast-iteration calibration target** for in-sprint scaffold work where the in-sprint model's language portfolio is Python-only and contamination is bounded by the in-sprint model's known cutoff.
- **Cross-reference**: P-122 anchors the **language-agnostic contamination-aware evaluation lineage** that supplements the existing SWE-bench family (P-111 / P-109 / P-118) and the V1 contamination-aware substrate (P-119) with the language-axis dimension the static benchmarks and the Python-only V1 substrate lack. Add P-122 to PRIM-22, PRIM-27, PRIM-31 rows in `Software-Archaeology-Lineage.md` alongside P-119. This is the **sixth pillar** of MAgHARCM's evaluation substrate, sitting alongside [[1.0.0 P-111]] (full SWE-bench), [[1.0.0 P-109]] (Verified), [[1.0.0 P-118]] (Lite), [[1.0.0 P-56]] (Multi-SWE-bench multilingual extension), [[1.0.0 P-119]] (V1 contamination-aware substrate), and [[1.0.0 P-120]] SWE-smith (synthetic-task generator).

## Hop-1 References (papers cited by Badertdinov et al. in V2)

- Jimenez et al. (2024) — SWE-bench [[1.0.0 P-111]] (the Python-only predecessor; V2's structural criteria are inherited from SWE-bench's failing-to-passing test transition contract).
- OpenAI (2024) — SWE-bench Verified [[1.0.0 P-109]] (the 500-instance human-curated subset; V2's per-language solvability filters are derived from Verified's solvability methodology).
- Jimenez et al. (2024) — SWE-bench Lite [[1.0.0 P-118]] (the 300-instance fast-iteration subset; V2's per-iteration cost model is calibrated against Lite's cost/iteration ratio).
- Zan et al. (2025) — Multi-SWE-bench [[1.0.0 P-56]] (the multilingual extension; V2's per-language issue-harvesting methodology, per-language Docker base images, and per-language test-runner adapters are built directly on Multi-SWE-bench's multilingual substrate).
- Badertdinov et al. (2025) — SWE-Rebench V1 [[1.0.0 P-119]] (the Python-only predecessor; V2's contamination provenance tracking, `created_at` / `training_cutoff` model, and per-model effective sample size computation are inherited unchanged from V1).
- Yang et al. (2024) — SWE-agent [[1.0.0 P-112]] (one of the three canonical evaluation scaffolds that V2 supports out-of-the-box across every per-language substrate).
- Wang et al. (2024) — OpenHands/CodeAct [[1.0.0 P-115]] (the multi-turn generalist scaffold that V2 supports alongside the procedural Agentless scaffold and the tool-calling SWE-agent scaffold on every per-language substrate).
